title: What the platform does
text: CRA-Native Product Security OS for European Software Companies (v1 focus) The platform is a B2B Product Security & Compliance SaaS built for European software, IoT, embedded, and connected-product companies . It helps engineering and security teams continuously understand: what software products they have; what components and dependencies those products contain; which vulnerabilities affect them; which releases and production environments are exposed; what security policies are being violated; what needs to be fixed; what evidence is required for CRA and other compliance frameworks. Product Security + CI/CD Security + CRA Compliance in one operational platform. Not a generic AppSec scanner, not a generic GRC platform. Core structure Organization → Workspaces → Teams → Projects → Products / Services → Environments. Each project connects its own repositories (GitHub / GitLab / Azure DevOps), CI/CD pipelines, Jira project, container registries, Kubernetes environments, security tools, cloud resources. Product inventory Product → Service → Repository → Build → Release → Container → Dependency → Deployment → Environment. SBOM management Per product and release: components, dependency versions, transitive dependencies, licenses, vulnerabilities, changes between releases (Product 4.1 → SBOM, 4.2 → SBOM, 4.3 → SBOM). Vulnerability management Continuous correlation of vulnerability intelligence with customer products: which products, versions, repositories, container images, environments are affected; whether production is exposed; which team owns it. "CVE-X affects Product A versions 3.2 and 3.3, 6 repositories, 2 container images, and the production Kubernetes deployment." Product Security Graph Products → Services → Repositories → Builds → Components → Containers → Deployments → Environments → Vulnerabilities → Teams: the actual business and technical impact of a security issue. Risk analysis CVSS, active exploitation, exploit availability, production exposure, internet exposure, product criticality, environment, customer impact, compensating controls. Same vulnerability: development → Medium; internet-facing production → Critical. Security policies No Critical vulnerabilities in Production; SBOM required before release; security scan required; approved dependencies / licenses only; container scan required; branch protection required; mandatory code review. Inherited Organization → Workspace → Team → Project. CI/CD security gates Push → Build → Tests → Security Scan → SBOM → Vulnerability Analysis → Policy Evaluation → PASS / FAIL → Deployment. A violated policy blocks the pipeline with policy, component and CVE named. Security runners Runners are the Execution Plane, the SaaS the Control Plane: scheduler → runner → scan → results. Managed runners for smaller customers; self-hosted runners inside enterprise infrastructure (code never has to leave; only findings, SBOM metadata and evidence come back; outbound HTTPS only, no public IP). Remediation Vulnerability detected → product impact → responsible team → remediation task → SLA → fix → new build scanned → verified → evidence stored → finding closed. Jira integration. CRA-native compliance and continuous evidence SBOM, vulnerability management, security update process, incident workflow, security testing, remediation history → CRA evidence, collected continuously and versioned from repositories, CI/CD, scans, runners, issue tracking, infrastructure, releases. Later: NIS2, ISO 27001, SOC 2, DORA. Agentic AI security consultant 24/7 consultant working only through platform tools and data, respecting RBAC: highest risks, products affected by CVE-X, why a pipeline failed, what to fix first, missing CRA evidence, what changed in 24 h. Controlled actions (analyze, prioritize, create remediation tasks, collect evidence, generate reports, explain policy failures, trigger approved scans); sensitive actions need human approval. Initial product scope Workspaces / Projects → GitHub / GitLab integrations → Managed / Self-Hosted Runners → Product Inventory → SBOM → Vulnerability Correlation → Product Security Graph → Risk Analysis → Security Policies → CI/CD Security Gates → Remediation → CRA Evidence → Agentic AI Consultant. Core lifecycle: Code → Build → Runner → SBOM → Vulnerability → Product Impact → Risk → Policy → Remediation → CRA Evidence → AI Automation. Initial customer: European company building its own software / IoT / embedded / connected products, 30–500 employees, several engineering teams, GitHub / GitLab / Azure DevOps, regular releases, preparing for CRA.

title: Roles and permissions
headings: Token scopes (personal tokens, matelot login, claude.ai connectors)
text: Roles, permissions and token scopes Roles (memberships) A membership gives a user a role on an organization, workspace, team or project; roles inherit downward. Role Can ORG_ADMIN everything in the organization SECURITY_ADMIN security administration: policies, SLAs, channels, connections, exceptions (request + approve), decisions, remediations COMPLIANCE_OFFICER reads + compliance / evidence writes, approve exceptions CISO reads + accept risk, approve exceptions, incidents, memberships CTO reads + structure writes (workspaces, teams, projects) TEAM_LEAD team structure, services, environments, decisions, remediations, request exceptions, pipelines PRODUCT_SECURITY_ENGINEER decisions, remediations and issues, request exceptions, pipelines, SBOMs DEVELOPER pipelines, SBOMs, deployments, request exceptions, reads AUDITOR / READ_ONLY / EXTERNAL_CONSULTANT reads Exceptions are time-boxed risk acceptances, not policies: exception:write (request/create, revoke your own) and exception:approve (make one active) are separate from policy:write . An exception created by someone who can approve is active at once; otherwise it waits for an approver (Project → Security → Exceptions → Approve). Token scopes (personal tokens, matelot login , claude.ai connectors) A token acts as the user, but the scope caps what the user's roles allow. Administrative roles are downgraded : Scope Effective role for ORG_ADMIN / SECURITY_ADMIN memberships Cell admins without memberships read AUDITOR AUDITOR on every organization write PRODUCT_SECURITY_ENGINEER PRODUCT_SECURITY_ENGINEER on every organization sudo unchanged (ORG_ADMIN); platform-admin elevation applies everything Other roles are unchanged by write (a DEVELOPER's write token is a DEVELOPER); read tokens are read-only on every route. Scope × action (asserted by apps/api/src/rbac/token-scope-matrix.spec.ts ) Action read write sudo read findings / gates / evidence ✅ ✅ ✅ decide on a finding ❌ ✅ ✅ create / update a remediation, open an issue ❌ ✅ ✅ request an exception ❌ ✅ ✅ approve an exception ❌ ❌ ✅ create a policy ❌ ❌ ✅ create a notification channel ❌ ❌ ✅ change SLA settings ❌ ❌ ✅ run a pipeline ❌ ✅ ✅ grant a membership ❌ ❌ ✅ The OAuth consent page ( /oauth/consent ) and matelot_start_here describe exactly this table.

title: Service coverage
text: Service coverage Two separate questions: Organization setup ( matelot onboarding , the "Set up your organization" card) covers one-time, organization-level steps: connect source code, get a runner working, and optionally send alerts somewhere and invite the team. Only administrators see it. Once completed it never comes back. Service coverage ( matelot coverage , the Coverage pages) asks whether every service is under watch. It never "completes": a new service starts with gaps, and a service that has not been scanned for a while goes stale. Counting "at least one somewhere in the organization" hid gaps. 3 of 4 services with a repository read as "done". Coverage is counted per service. Checks (per service) Check ok when otherwise repository a repository is attached to the service gap: matelot repository attach --service <id> --repository-id <id> pipeline a pipeline of the service finished (succeeded or failed) within the last N days (default 30, --days / ?days= 1–365) stale when the last one finished earlier, gap when none ever finished: matelot pipeline --service <id> --template security --wait sbom the service has an SBOM gap: matelot sbom --service <id> --file bom.json --target source (or run the pipeline) policy an enabled policy applies: on the service or one of its environments, or inherited from its project, team, workspace or organization gap: matelot policy from-template-project --project <id> --template production-baseline deployment a deployment of the service was recorded in any environment gap: matelot deploy --env <id> --image <ref> (or matelot env create … first when the service has no environment) Every gap comes with the web page that fixes it and the CLI command with the ids filled in. Where Project → Coverage : one row per service, a check or a gap per column. Under each uncovered row are the commands that close its gaps. It follows the project's service selector. Overview → Service coverage : e.g. "3/4 with a repository · 2/4 scanned in the last 30 days · …". Each number links to /coverage?gap=<check> , the uncovered services across the organization filtered by that check. Visible to everyone who can read the project. The organization view counts only the projects the viewer can read. API GET /projects/:projectId/coverage?days=&gap=&uncovered=true ( project:read ) returns { projectId, days, summary, services[] } . GET /organizations/:organizationId/coverage?days=&gap=&limit= ( organization:read , filtered per project by project:read ) returns { days, gap, summary, uncoveredTotal, uncovered[] } . gap narrows the list but never the summary. summary = { services, covered, checks: { <check>: { ok, stale, missing } } } . Each service has { covered, gaps[], checks[]: { id, state: ok|stale|missing, detail, href, cli } } . CLI matelot coverage # organization: per-check counts + services with gaps matelot coverage --gap pipeline # only services not scanned in the window matelot coverage --project <id> # the project's table matelot coverage --project <id> --uncovered # only the gaps, each with the command that fixes it matelot coverage --days 7 --json

title: CI/CD integration
headings: External registries (Docker Hub, GHCR, GitLab, Harbor…)
AWS ECR and Azure Container Registry
Gate timing in CI: wait for correlation
text:
CI/CD integration (signed CI tokens) Pipelines talk to the platform with CI tokens : machine credentials created on a project (or team / workspace / organization), limited to what a pipeline needs, revocable, audited. Requests are signed , never carry the secret, cannot be replayed or altered: Authorization: SecOps-HMAC-SHA256 keyId=sk_…,ts=<unix>,nonce=<random>,sig=<hex> sig = HMAC-SHA256(secret, "v1
" + ts + "
" + nonce + "
" + METHOD + "
" + path + "
" + sha256hex(body)) The cell accepts a timestamp within ±5 minutes and each nonce once (Redis). The secret is shown once at creation and stored encrypted with the cell key. Create a token Project → Settings → CI tokens → New token → choose a preset ( Report releases and deployments , Run security pipelines and gates , Everything a pipeline can do ), optional expiry → copy keyId and secret into your CI secrets ( MATELOT_KEY_ID , MATELOT_SECRET ). Use it npm package secops-platform-cli (source: apps/cli , published from github.com/dev-testing-secops-platform/secops-platform-cli ; Node ≥ 18): npx secops-platform-cli deploy … , or in GitHub Actions the repository's action, which installs it and exports the variables: - uses: dev-testing-secops-platform/secops-platform-cli@main # or @v2.6.0 with: url: ${{ vars.MATELOT_URL }} key-id: ${{ secrets.MATELOT_KEY_ID }} secret: ${{ secrets.MATELOT_SECRET }} - run: matelot pipeline --service ${{ vars.MATELOT_SERVICE_ID }} --ref ${{ github.sha }} --wait - run: matelot deploy --env ${{ vars.MATELOT_ENV_PROD }} --version ${{ github.ref_name }} --image $IMAGE GitLab CI and Bitbucket Pipelines equivalents: `docs/examples/gitlab-ci.yml`, `docs/examples/bitbucket-pipelines.yml`. A complete GitHub workflow (pipeline on every push, dev on main, tag → test → blocking prod gate → prod → signed evidence artifact) is in `docs/examples/github-actions.yml`. The action installs the CLI from the GitHub repository (`npm install -g github:…#ref`), so no npm publish is needed. Releases: git tag cli-v0.1.0 && git push --tags runs .github/workflows/publish-cli.yml , which publishes to npm with provenance (Sigstore attestation linking the package to the commit and workflow), so consumers can verify what they run ( npm audit signatures ). Requires an NPM_TOKEN secret (automation token of the npm org) once. For the rare CI without Node, tools/secops-ci/secops.sh (bash + openssl + curl) implements the same protocol (not advertised in the UI): - uses: <org>/secops-platform/tools/secops-ci@main with: url: https://acme.secops.example.com key-id: ${{ secrets.MATELOT_KEY_ID }} secret: ${{ secrets.MATELOT_SECRET }} command: deploy args: --env 3f2a… --version ${{ github.ref_name }} --image ghcr.io/acme/app:${{ github.ref_name }} GitLab CI / Jenkins / anything else: curl -sSO https://…/secops.sh && bash secops.sh deploy … . Commands: whoami , deploy --env <id> --version X [--image ref] , release --service <id> --version X , pipeline --service <id> [--template security] [--ref <branch|tag|sha>] , sbom --service <id> --file bom.json --target source|image [--version X] [--image ref] (upload an SBOM the CI generated itself, e.g. syft dir:. -o cyclonedx-json=bom.json or syft ghcr.io/acme/app:1.2.0 -o cyclonedx-json=bom.json with the job's own registry access), request METHOD /api/v1/… '<json>' . Network The CI job needs outbound HTTPS to the cell. Hosted CI runners (github.com) require the cell to be reachable from the internet (TLS terminates in the cell, so the connection is end-to-end encrypted); a private cell works with self-hosted CI runners. For customers who require it, the cell ingress can additionally demand a client certificate (mTLS). Built-in registry Namespaces mirror the platform, like GitLab group paths — no collisions between teams and the path says who owns the image: <workspace>/<team>/<project>/<service>:<tag> builds (scanned on every push) <workspace>/<team>/<project>/<service>/<environment>:<tag> deployed to that environment Pushing into an environment repository — or matelot promote --env <id> --tag <tag> , which copies the build inside the registry without re-uploading — is the deployment; the cluster pulls from the environment repository. A project CI token may use only its project's namespace. Protected environments (Environments → Settings → Protected ): only CI tokens explicitly allowed for that environment ( Settings → CI tokens → May deploy to ) can push/promote into it or record deployments there; a build token therefore cannot deploy to production by accident. Give the release job its own token. Nothing is hard-coded in pipelines: matelot registry login logs Docker in with the CI token, matelot registry path --service <id> prints the build image path ( --env <id> the environment path), matelot promote deploys. Every environment row in the UI has copy buttons for its registry path and id; templates with the real values are under Environments → CI snippet (GitHub Actions and GitLab CI). With the preset Push and pull images (or Everything a pipeline can do ), the same CI token is a Docker credential: docker login <registry host> -u $MATELOT_KEY_ID -p $MATELOT_SECRET . Repository paths follow <project-slug>/<service-slug>[/<name>]:<tag> ; a project token may only push under its project. Every push is recorded (tag, digest) on the service and an image SBOM is generated. External registries (Docker Hub, GHCR, GitLab, Harbor…) Connect the registry once ( Integrations → Connect a source → Container registry : host, robot/read token). The pipeline pushes there as usual and reports what it deployed: - run: matelot deploy --env $MATELOT_ENV_DEV --image docker.io/acme/app@sha256:<digest from the push> - run: matelot deploy --env $MATELOT_ENV_PRODUCTION --version v1.7.0 --image docker.io/acme/app:v1.7.0 The first report registers the image on the service; tags and digests are read through the connection every 15 minutes; tags link to releases by version or commit; every reported tag and every tag that appears after the first sync gets an image SBOM automatically (the historical backlog is scanned on demand). promote exists only for the built-in registry — external registries have no environment repositories, so the deploy step reports instead. Protected environments apply to matelot deploy through the token's May deploy to . AWS ECR and Azure Container Registry Connect them like any registry ( Integrations → Connect a source → AWS Elastic Container Registry / Azure Container Registry ), but with an IAM access key (ECR) or a service principal (ACR) instead of a Docker password. The platform exchanges those for short-lived Docker credentials — 12-hour ECR tokens via GetAuthorizationToken (SigV4), ~3-hour ACR refresh tokens via the AAD → /oauth2/exchange flow — for tag sync, image scanning by runners, and CI logins. The AWS/Azure secret never leaves the cell. In CI, no cloud CLI or cloud credential is needed on the runner: - run: matelot registry login --connection "ECR · production" --service $MATELOT_SERVICE_ID - run: | IMAGE=$(matelot registry path --service $MATELOT_SERVICE_ID --connection "ECR · production" --repository app --create) docker build -t $IMAGE:$GITHUB_SHA . && docker push $IMAGE:$GITHUB_SHA - run: matelot deploy --env $MATELOT_ENV_DEV --image <image>@sha256:… registry path --connection … --repository … resolves the host from the connection (nothing to configure in CI); --create makes the ECR repository if it does not exist (token needs registry:push ). matelot registry connections --service <id> lists the connections on the service's path. Issuing credentials requires registry:pull (CI presets registry / pipeline / full ; people with deploy rights) and is recorded in the audit trail. Minimal cloud rights: ECR — ecr:GetAuthorizationToken , ecr:BatchGetImage , ecr:GetDownloadUrlForLayer , ecr:ListImages , ecr:DescribeImages ecr:DescribeRepositories (+ ecr:CreateRepository to create repositories from the platform: connection → Manage → ECR repositories ; + ecr:PutImage / InitiateLayerUpload / UploadLayerPart / CompleteLayerUpload for pushes); ACR — role AcrPull (+ AcrPush ). Installing the CLI in CI The CLI reads MATELOT_URL , MATELOT_KEY_ID , MATELOT_SECRET (CI token) or MATELOT_TOKEN (personal token), and MATELOT_COMMIT for deploy . The old SECOPS_* names are still accepted as a fallback. dev-testing-secops-platform/secops-platform-cli is a private repository, so uses: …@main and npm install -g github:… only work for runners that can read it. For other organizations, pick one: Package tarball : npm pack in the CLI repository produces matelot-cli-<version>.tgz ; host it where runners can download it (an internal artifact store, a release asset) and install with npm install -g <url-or-path>.tgz . Internal npm registry (Verdaccio, Artifactory, GitHub Packages): npm publish there, then npm install -g matelot-cli . Public npm : once the package name is decided and published, npm install -g <name> works everywhere. The GitHub Action is a thin wrapper around the install; replace its uses: step with a run: npm install -g … line plus the three environment variables when the action is not reachable. Gate timing in CI: wait for correlation Right after docker push , the image's SBOM is still being correlated for a few seconds. matelot gate and matelot deploy therefore wait for it ( --wait-correlation N seconds; default 300 in CI — detected by the CI variable or a CI token — and 0 for a person at a terminal) and only then evaluate the policies. The CLI asks the server in short slices (≤ 25 s per request, so no ingress or load balancer timeout is hit) until the budget is spent: "waiting for SBOM correlation… (50 s / 300 s)" lines go to stderr. It also waits for the image's SBOM to exist : right after a push the SBOM job may not have run, and an image nobody scanned never passes a gate, even where the policies do not require an SBOM. Exit codes: 0 pass/warn · 2 a blocking policy failed · 3 not evaluated (no SBOM for the image after the budget, or its correlation still pending or failed; no counts are printed, nothing was judged) · 4 authentication. Let a 3 fail the job loudly (the platform could not tell), but do not treat it as a security verdict. Breaking change in CLI 2.9.0: an authentication failure now exits 4 (it was 3 ); 3 means "not evaluated". Scripts that tested for 3 to detect a bad token must test for 4 . Pipeline jobs Stage Job Tool Needs source checkout git repository access (connection) inventory sbom syft — scan dependencies ( sca ) platform correlation (OSV / NVD / KEV / EPSS) the sbom job scan code ( sast ) Semgrep ( --config auto ; set SEMGREP_CONFIG=p/ci on an offline runner) runner image ≥ this release scan secrets, infrastructure trivy — policy evaluate ( policy_eval ) platform worker — Rebuild the runner image after this release ( docker build apps/runner ) so semgrep is present; a runner without it reports the code job as skipped with that reason.

title: Access tokens
text: Access tokens Token For Acts as Reach CI token (project → Settings → CI tokens) pipelines the token itself its scope (project/team/…), its preset, its May deploy to list Personal access token (user menu → Access tokens) people: scripts, the API, secops on a laptop the user see scopes below Personal token scopes read — GET / HEAD only, within the user's memberships. write — the full API as the user, within the user's workspace / team / project memberships . Organization-admin and security-admin roles and the platform admin flag are not carried. sudo — administrators only: the user's full rights, including organization / platform administration. A normal user's token therefore reaches exactly the projects they are assigned to. An admin's everyday token behaves like a member token; admin power is opt-in per (short-lived) sudo token. Security properties spt_ + 240 random bits; only the SHA-256 is stored; shown once. Expiry 1–365 days; revocable; last use (time, IP) tracked. A personal token cannot create or revoke tokens (sign in to the web app); CI tokens neither. Created / revoked events are audited in every organization the user belongs to. Everything done with a token is audited as the user. Use curl -H "Authorization: Bearer spt_…" https://<cell>/api/v1/me export SECOPS_URL=https://<cell> SECOPS_TOKEN=spt_… # matelot CLI as yourself matelot whoami The built-in registry docker login still uses a CI token ( matelot registry login with SECOPS_KEY_ID/SECRET). API collection and checks tools/api/ : secops-api-check.mjs (calls every GET endpoint with your token and reports PASS / DENIED / FAIL), secops.postman_collection.json and secops.http (every operation), README.md (everyday curl calls).

title: MCP server (AI assistants)
headings: What Claude can do with it
Parity with the web app and the CLI
text: MCP server — use Matelot from Claude The API embeds an MCP server (Streamable HTTP, stateless) at POST /api/v1/mcp . Every REST endpoint is exposed as a tool, generated from the OpenAPI document at boot, so anything added to the API is available to Claude without extra work. Tool names follow the controller and method ( vulnerabilities_project_summary , remediation_project_queue , policies_from_template_project , remediation_issue , cra_readiness_service , notification_channels_create_project , …); scoped routes get one tool per scope ( …_workspaces , …_teams ). Auth Personal access tokens (Account → Access tokens; spt_… ): read — Claude can query everything (findings, gate results, fix-first queue, risk, CRA readiness, evidence summaries) and cannot change anything: non-GET tools are refused by the MCP layer. write — Claude can also create exceptions, remediations, issues, policies, channels, run pipelines. sudo — administrators only. Calls run through the normal HTTP layer: the same RBAC (your memberships), validation and audit trail apply, attributed to your user. A session JWT from the web app also works. Per-user behaviour The MCP is the user's own view of the platform, derived from their token on every request: Token Who Tools listed Can change web session or sudo token of a platform administrator cell admin all (incl. admin_* , organizations, runners) everything write token regular member everything except admin routes only inside their workspace / team / project memberships (organization-admin roles do not count on these tokens, by design) read token regular member GET tools only nothing On initialize the instructions include an identity block ("You are acting as … — regular member / platform administrator", token scope, memberships with ids), so Claude knows which scopes it may talk about and does not guess outside them. Tools that are hidden are also refused if called by name. Every call is authorised by the API's RBAC with the same rules as the web app and CLI, and audited under the user. Connect matelot mcp # prints the snippets for your cell matelot mcp --check # handshake + tool count Claude Code: claude mcp add --transport http matelot https://matelot.example.com/api/v1/mcp --header "Authorization: Bearer spt_…" Claude Desktop ( claude_desktop_config.json ): { "mcpServers": { "matelot": { "type": "http", "url": "https://matelot.example.com/api/v1/mcp", "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer spt_…" } } } } claude.ai (web and mobile): Settings → Connectors → Add custom connector → URL https://<your cell>/api/v1/mcp . No token to paste: claude.ai discovers the cell's OAuth server ( /.well-known/oauth-authorization-server ), registers itself, sends you to Matelot's consent page where you choose read-only / read & write, and receives a token that is a personal access token of yours (revocable under Account → Access tokens; refreshed automatically). The cell must be reachable from the internet over HTTPS, and API_PUBLIC_URL must be set to that public URL. CLI without pasting tokens: matelot login --url https://<your cell> opens the browser for the same consent and stores the token in ~/.config/matelot/credentials.json (refreshed when it expires; matelot logout revokes it). What Claude can do with it "Why is payment-api blocked in prod?" → gate evaluation → failing rule → the findings behind it → existing exceptions. "What should we fix first this sprint?" → remediation queue for the workspace, grouped by service. "Track the top three and open Jira issues" → remediation_create + remediation_issue (asks before writing). "Draft an exception for CVE-2024-1234 in demo, 90 days, reason: not reachable" → policies_create_exception_service . "Are we CRA-ready for release 1.9.9?" → cra_readiness_service + evidence_summary . "Which services still run an image with a KEV in production?" → vulnerabilities_environments_org with kev=true . The server's instructions text (sent on initialize) explains the hierarchy, how to discover ids and to confirm before any change; deployments are meant to stay in CI. Parity with the web app and the CLI The MCP tool set is generated from the OpenAPI document, so it is exactly the public API. apps/api/src/parity.spec.ts asserts that every web-app action goes through a documented route (= an MCP tool) and that every mutating route also has a matelot command. Anything you can click, Claude can do (within the token's permissions), and so can a script. docs/parity-matrix.md lists every route with its UI / API / CLI / MCP coverage. Working with large answers Every GET tool accepts two extra parameters handled by the MCP layer: max_items (default 50, max 500) keeps only the first N items of a list, fields (comma-separated) keeps only those keys on each item. When a list is cut, the answer starts with "Showing N of M items…". Use the tool's own filters (severity, status, kev, q, running) to narrow first. Output is compact JSON, capped at 60 kB. matelot_start_here (always first in the tool list) returns the server instructions and the identity block, for clients that do not surface the initialize instructions to the model. Implementation apps/api/src/mcp/ : mcp.service.ts (tool generation from the OpenAPI document, execution via loopback HTTP with the caller's Authorization header, output truncation at 60 kB), mcp.controller.ts (JSON-RPC: initialize, ping, tools/list, tools/call; notifications → 202; GET → 405). Excluded routes: auth, oauth, health, runner protocol, webhooks, registry v2, binary downloads. main.ts passes the OpenAPI document to McpService.load . Read-only personal tokens are allowed to POST to /mcp only (transport); the MCP layer enforces GET-only tools for them.

title: GitHub App
headings: Own GitHub App: flow, pitfalls, checklist
text: Own GitHub App: flow, pitfalls, checklist Slug and name come from GitHub ( GET /app ) at connect time; the slug you type is only a hint and a mismatch is reported. The install link is always built from GitHub's slug. The Name field is a display label. Retries update the pending connection of the same App at the same level instead of creating another one. Already installed? GitHub then opens the installation settings instead of the Setup URL, so no callback arrives. Matelot lists the App's installations on connect and binds the one that fits; otherwise use Manage → Actions → Link existing installation . The callback also handles setup_action=update . Expired link : install links are signed for 15 minutes. If GitHub sends you back later, the Connections page explains and offers "Link existing installation". Two URLs : Setup URL / Redirect URI ( …/api/v1/integrations/github/callback , browser GET) vs Webhook URL ( …/api/v1/webhooks/github/<connection id> , GitHub servers POST). A GET on the webhook URL now returns an explanation instead of 404. Webhooks are verified with X-Hub-Signature-256 , deduplicated on X-GitHub-Delivery , acknowledged with 202 and processed asynchronously. localhost / private hosts : GitHub cannot deliver webhooks there. Use a tunnel (smee.io, ngrok, Tailscale Funnel) or click Later: the connection works without webhooks, with Sync now and periodic polling. Permissions : Repository — Metadata read, Contents read, Administration read, Issues read & write; Organization — Projects read & write (boards). Granted permissions are read from the installation and missing ones are listed in Manage → Details; after adding permissions to the App, the organization must accept them (Organization → Settings → GitHub Apps), then Check again . Capabilities by connection type : deploy key / plain git → clone only, no issues or boards; fine-grained token → issues and user- or organization-owned boards; GitHub App → issues and organization-owned boards only (a /users/… board is skipped with a log message). One App per environment (dev behind a tunnel, staging, prod): an App has a single webhook URL and separate keys limit the blast radius. Test checklist Connect with a wrong slug hint → connection created, warning shows GitHub's slug, Install link uses it. Connect the same App twice at the same level → second attempt updates the first pending record (no duplicates). Install the App on GitHub first, then connect → bound immediately, status pending → connected after the first sync. Wait > 15 min on the GitHub install page, then continue → Connections page shows the expired-link banner; Link existing installation completes it. curl -i https://<host>/api/v1/webhooks/github/<id> → 200 with the explanation, not 404. Remove Issues write from the App → Manage → Check again lists it as missing; add it back, accept on GitHub, Check again → clean. App connection + /users/<you>/projects/1 board → issue created, log says user boards need a token connection.

title: Keyless registry access
text: Keyless registry connections (workload identity federation) Matelot can pull from Google Artifact Registry, Amazon ECR and Azure Container Registry without storing a cloud secret. The platform is an OIDC identity provider; each connection gets its own identity, and the cloud trusts tokens Matelot signs for it. How it works Issuer: API_PUBLIC_URL (must be public HTTPS — the cloud fetches the discovery document and keys). Discovery: <issuer>/.well-known/openid-configuration , keys: <issuer>/.well-known/jwks.json . Tokens: RS256, 10-minute lifetime, sub = integration:<connection id> , one audience per cloud. The signing key is stored encrypted with the cell key. If it can no longer be decrypted (cell key changed) a new key is generated; the old public key stays in the JWKS as retired. Cloud Auth type Audience Exchange GCP (GAR) gcp_wif https://iam.googleapis.com/<provider resource> STS token exchange → generateAccessToken for the service account → docker user oauth2accesstoken AWS (ECR) aws_wif sts.amazonaws.com AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity → temporary keys → ECR GetAuthorizationToken Azure (ACR) azure_wif api://AzureADTokenExchange Entra ID client credentials with a client assertion → ACR refresh token Setting it up The cloud trusts the exact subject integration:<connection id> , and the id only exists once the connection is created. So a keyless connection is created first, unverified, and checked afterwards: Create the connection with Keyless on (web: Connect → registry → Keyless), or via CLI matelot connection create --body '{"provider":"registry","baseUrl":"…","auth":{"type":"aws_wif","roleArn":"…","region":"…"}}' . Nothing is probed and nothing is signed at this point; the connection is pending with settings.verified=false , and the response carries identity (issuer, subject, audience, steps). "Test connection" is not available for keyless connections for the same reason. Configure the trust in the cloud for that subject. Manage → Identity · keyless (or matelot connection identity --id <connection> ) shows the concrete values: GCP : workload identity pool + OIDC provider with the issuer URL, mapping google.subject=assertion.sub ; then gcloud iam service-accounts add-iam-policy-binding SA --role=roles/iam.workloadIdentityUser --member="principal://iam.googleapis.com/<pool>/subject/integration:<id>" (the principal is filled in from the connection's provider path); the service account needs Artifact Registry Reader. AWS : IAM OIDC identity provider (issuer URL, audience sts.amazonaws.com ); the role's trust policy is shown as JSON with StringEquals { "<issuer host>:aud": "sts.amazonaws.com", "<issuer host>:sub": "integration:<id>" } ; attach AmazonEC2ContainerRegistryReadOnly . Azure : a federated credential on the app registration — issuer, subject integration:<id> (exact match), audience api://AzureADTokenExchange ; the az ad app federated-credential create command is shown ready to paste. Give the app AcrPull on the registry. Verify : the Verify button (Identity tab, the wizard's last step, or Manage → Actions), or matelot connection verify --id <connection> . It signs a token for the real subject and runs the exchange. A refusal is stored as the connection's last error and shown under Identity; success sets verified and starts the first sync. Until then syncs of the connection are a quiet no-op (no error state). The cell never signs a token for a placeholder subject: a keyless exchange without a real connection id is refused before any cloud call. Disconnect and delete matelot connection disconnect --id X ( POST /integrations/:id/disconnect ) keeps the connection and its repositories but forgets the credentials. A disconnected keyless connection shows only "Disconnected — create the connection again" with its non-secret parameters (client id, role ARN, provider / service account); it cannot be verified. matelot connection delete --id X ( DELETE /integrations/:id ) removes the connection, its repositories and their service links. If container images pull through it, the API answers 409 listing them; --force (web: "Detach images and delete") detaches them, and their next sync looks for another usable connection to the same registry. Status: a verified keyless connection becomes connected (pending reason cleared) after its first successful sync, source or image. Disconnected and unverified keyless connections are never picked for image pulls. The issuer must be reachable by the cloud provider. With API_PUBLIC_URL unset or not HTTPS, the Identity page shows a warning and verification will fail at the cloud's token exchange.

title: Builds, releases, deployments
headings: Built-in registry: what records a deployment
text: Release process — how builds, releases and environments connect The model Concept What it is Created by Build an image built from a commit ( <registry>/<repo>:<commit> ), identified by its digest a push to the platform registry, or a deployment that reports it Release a version of the service ( 1.9.0 ), tied to a commit a deployment that names a version ( matelot deploy --version ), a git tag / GitHub or GitLab release sync, or Record release Deployment "this image / release now runs in this environment" matelot deploy , matelot promote , a push to an environment repository, Kubernetes sync A release does not have an environment — a deployment puts it there. One release can run in several environments (test, then prod, then a DR region); the graph draws release → image → environment for every current deployment. Standard flow commit ──build──► image demo:<sha> ──deploy──► dev (no release: a build of main) tag v1.9.0-rc1 ──► image …:v1.9.0-rc1 ──deploy──► test release 1.9.0-rc1 created by the deployment tag v1.9.0 ──► image …:v1.9.0 ──deploy──► prod release 1.9.0 created by the deployment Every deploy step reports --version (for rc and final), --image <image>@<digest> and --commit . What the platform guarantees A deployment that names a version creates the release if it does not exist yet (version-like names only), with the commit from --commit / SECOPS_COMMIT ; audited as release.created . Git tag sync later enriches the same release (URL, notes, date) — it no longer depends on webhooks reaching the cell. A digest is one image , whatever registry or tag it lives under: a deployment reported by digest from a registry the platform has not read yet triggers an immediate registry read, and every later sync attaches digest-only deployments to their tag; the security graph, Vulnerabilities → Running in , the trend snapshots and the correlation all resolve "what runs here" by digest; the same image pushed to several registries is scanned once (one SBOM per digest). Tags link to releases by version ( v1.9.0 ↔ 1.9.0 ), by commit ( <sha> tags), and by a deployment that names both a version and an image. Built-in registry: what records a deployment matelot promote records the deployment itself, the moment the copy is done (no dependency on registry notifications reaching the API or on the reconcile loop). A real docker push into an environment repository is recorded by the registry notification. The reconcile pass (every 2 minutes, or POST /organizations/:id/registry/reconcile ) only fills an environment that has nothing recorded, or records a tag built after the current deployment (a push the notification missed). It never overwrites a deployment reported from another registry, by hand or by Kubernetes — older tags lying in the environment repository are ignored. All three paths are serialised per environment, so they cannot record the same deployment twice. Environment lineage (Security graph → Environments) Per environment, two lanes: Released — repository (commit) → release (version tag) → registries holding that tag → environment; Running now — repository (commit of the running build) → image digest → registries holding that digest (the one it was deployed from marked) → environment. Only the digest identifies what runs; a tag is a pointer that can move. Drift is flagged when the lanes disagree: the version tag was rebuilt after the deployment ( tag_moved ), the tag points to different images in different registries ( tag_split ), the running digest is in no known registry ( unknown_image ), no release exists for the deployed version ( no_release ), the running image was never scanned ( not_scanned ), a registry sync fails. API: GET /environments/:id/lineage . Where to see it Releases & images (release card: images + environment chips) · Running now · Security graph (hover a release) · Vulnerabilities → Running in · Audit ( release.created , deployment.recorded ).

title: Managed runners
text: Managed runners A fresh cell runs pipelines without the customer installing anything: the Helm chart deploys the cell's own runner agents (a StatefulSet), which register into the Managed pool and run jobs for every organization and project of the cell. Self-hosted pools stay for jobs that must reach the customer's network (private git hosts, registries, Kubernetes clusters). How it works The chart generates MANAGED_RUNNER_SECRET on first install (Secret <release>-managed-runner , kept across upgrades like the encryption key) and gives it to the API and to the runners. On every start a managed runner registers with that secret ( POST /runner/register { managedSecret, name } ). The platform creates the Managed pool on first use (one per cell, under the bootstrap organization) and replaces the record of the same name, so pod restarts never pile up offline duplicates. If its token is no longer accepted (record removed), the agent registers again by itself. The Managed pool serves every organization of the cell (the claim skips the organization / scope filter for it); required tags still apply. It carries the tag managed ; the agent adds linux (and docker when it has a daemon). Managed runners get no Kubernetes API access, and the agent never adds the kubernetes tag by itself when it runs with RUNNER_MANAGED_SECRET (even though it runs inside a cluster and ships kubectl), so cluster-inventory jobs stay on customer runners. managedRunners.tags can still add it deliberately. While the API is unreachable (cell restore, upgrade, ingress reload) a managed runner keeps retrying registration, heartbeats and claims with backoff (2 s → 60 s) instead of exiting; only a definite answer such as a 401 (wrong secret) stops it. The pool is read-only for customers: it cannot be deleted and has no registration tokens. It is listed on every Runners page ("managed by the platform"). Runners of the Managed pool not seen for a day (scaled-down ordinals, deleted pods) are pruned by the worker; a busy runner never is. Usage: runner minutes are split — runnerMinutesManaged (and the CSV column runner_minutes_managed ) is the part run on managed runners. Helm values managedRunners: enabled: true # false removes the StatefulSet (the Secret is kept) replicas: 1 # 0 stops them image: { repository: secops-runner, tag: "" } # tag defaults to the chart appVersion tags: [] secret: "" # empty = generated and kept resources: { requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 512Mi }, limits: { cpu: "2", memory: 2Gi } } workDirSize: 4Gi make kind-load builds and loads the runner image; make deploy points managedRunners.image at it. Without the chart (local development): start the API with MANAGED_RUNNER_SECRET=<48 chars> and a runner with RUNNER_URL=… RUNNER_MANAGED_SECRET=<same> RUNNER_NAME=managed-0 node apps/runner/dist/index.js .

title: Runner protocol
text: Runner ↔ cell protocol (v1) A runner is a process (Docker container, VM service, Kubernetes pod) that executes jobs for one cell. It only ever makes outbound HTTPS calls to the cell's API ( <web url>/api/v1/runner/… ); the cell never connects to the runner, so runners work behind NAT and firewalls. Reference implementation: apps/runner (TypeScript); the protocol is small enough for a Go/Rust agent. Where to run it Docker, Docker Compose, a Kubernetes Deployment (manifest generated by the Register dialog), or from source. The runner needs outbound HTTPS to the platform and network access to what it scans (git host, registry, cluster). It does not need to share a network with the platform. Registration POST /runner/register { registrationToken | managedSecret, name, tags[], version, metadata } (self-hosted: a registration token from the Runners page; the cell's managed runners: MANAGED_RUNNER_SECRET , same name replaces the previous record — see managed-runners.md) → { runnerId, runnerToken, pool } . Registration tokens come from the Runners page (one-time, 24 h). The runner token ( rt_… ) is the runner's identity; keep it in a 0600 file/volume and present it as Authorization: Bearer rt_… on every other call. Liveness POST /runner/heartbeat every 15 s { metadata? } . A runner silent for 60 s is marked offline and its job is requeued. Getting work POST /runner/jobs/claim { waitSeconds ≤ 25 } — long poll. 200 with a job the cell has atomically assigned to this runner (matching: same organization, pool on the project's path, required_tags ⊆ pool.tags ∪ runner.tags , highest priority first, oldest first) or 204 . The assignment carries a 60 s lease. Running a job POST /runner/jobs/:id/start — job becomes running . POST /runner/jobs/:id/heartbeat every 20 s — extends the lease; the response says whether the job was cancelled (stop work, no completion call needed). POST /runner/jobs/:id/credentials — for repository jobs: { kind: 'https'|'ssh'|'none', url, username?/secret? | privateKey, defaultBranch, fullName } , minted just in time (GitHub App installation tokens live 1 h). Never persisted on the runner. POST /runner/jobs/:id/logs { chunks: [{ seq, stream: stdout|stderr|system, content }] } — batched, idempotent by seq . POST /runner/jobs/:id/complete { status: succeeded|failed|skipped, result?, error?, exitCode? } — skipped means "this runner does not implement the job type"; a pipeline treats it as non-failing. If the lease expires (runner crash), the sweeper requeues the job ( attempts < maxAttempts ) or fails it; jobs also time out at timeoutSeconds . Job types repository_check (clone, report HEAD/branch/size — the smoke test of the chain), custom , sbom (payload target: source|image , ref / imageRef , optional version : Syft → CycloneDX, uploaded with POST /runner/jobs/:id/sbom ; image jobs fetch registry credentials with POST /runner/jobs/:id/registry-credentials ), kubernetes_inventory (payload namespace , optional context : lists deployments / statefulsets / daemonsets / cronjobs and running-pod image digests with kubectl ; the cell turns matching images into deployments of the environment — requires a runner with cluster access, tag kubernetes ) ( payload.command run with sh -c , in the clone when a repository is attached). Step 04+ add sbom , sca , sast , secrets , iac , container_scan , … each with a results contract. Security properties Runners get only jobs created through the platform (RBAC-checked at creation); the token is bound to one pool and therefore one organization subtree. Credentials are fetched per job, kept in memory/temp files with 0600, deleted after the job. Logs are scrubbed of https://user:token@ and Authorization: Basic … before upload. Register and heartbeat responses carry config — registryHostAliases (the cell tells containerised runners of a local cell to reach localhost:5000 as host.docker.internal:5000 ; merged with the optional env REGISTRY_HOST_ALIASES ) and latestVersion (the agent warns when outdated; the Runners page flags it). Runners report metadata.container (from /.dockerenv or in-cluster) and their version on every heartbeat. Automatic image SBOMs are queued once per tag; after a failure the tag is not retried automatically for 12 hours (retry from the job page). Syft errors are reported verbatim in the job log and error field. secrets / iac jobs run Trivy offline on the checked-out repository and upload normalised findings with POST /runner/jobs/:id/code-findings ( { kind, ref, findings[] } ; evidence redacted on the runner and again in the cell). The cell closes findings of that kind that the scan no longer reports. Assignment guarantees A job is constrained only by the pool requested when it was created ( requested_pool_id ); where an attempt ran ( pool_id ) never binds a requeue. A claim whose connection closes is dropped; a job assigned to it, or whose claim response was not delivered, goes back to the queue at once without counting the attempt. An assignment not started within 30 s returns to the queue; a started job is requeued when its 60 s lease expires (up to maxAttempts ). On SIGTERM the agent aborts its open claim and never starts a new job.

title: Provisioning a cell
text: Provisioning a tenant cell Every customer gets one cell: a Helm release of deploy/helm/secops-cell in its own namespace tenant-<slug> , with its own API, web app, worker, managed runners, Postgres, Redis, Keycloak, registry and backups. Cells never share data. This runbook takes a cell from "signed contract" to "customer logged in", and covers upgrades and decommissioning. The control plane that will automate it later (roadmap step 17) will run the same steps. 1. Prerequisites (once per cluster) Need Why Check Kubernetes 1.28+, kubectl and helm 3 with access kubectl config current-context An ingress controller, class nginx by default one Ingress per host per cell kubectl get ingressclass cert-manager with a ClusterIssuer (e.g. letsencrypt ) TLS for <slug>.<domain> , auth-<slug>.<domain> , registry-<slug>.<domain> kubectl get clusterissuer A wildcard DNS record *.<domain> → the ingress one record covers every cell dig +short x.<domain> A default StorageClass (or set *.storageClassName ) Postgres, registry, backups kubectl get storageclass The three images in a registry the cluster can pull from secops-api , secops-web , secops-runner at the same tag imagePullSecrets per namespace if private For backups off-site: an S3 bucket and credentials or pod identity docs/backup-restore.md Optional: an SMTP relay for e-mail notifications api.extraEnv SMTP_* Cells are isolated by NetworkPolicy (nothing outside the namespace reaches a cell except the ingress controller), so the ingress controller's namespace must match ingress.controllerNamespace (default ingress-nginx ). 2. Inputs per cell Input Example Notes slug globex DNS label, immutable, becomes the namespace, release name, hostnames and root organization slug name Globex Corporation root organization display name domain platform.example.com the shared platform domain; hosts are derived from it admin e-mails ciso@globex.com first login of each becomes ORG_ADMIN of the root organization ( BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_EMAILS ) image tag 0.2.0 one tag for the three images database bundled or managed production: managed Postgres, postgres.bundled=false + externalUrl / externalKeycloakJdbcUrl secrets DB_PASSWORD , KC_ADMIN_PASSWORD , SMTP password… environment variables at apply time, never in the values file backups PVC and/or S3 prefix cells/<slug> on by default in the template 3. Create the cell scripts/cell-provision.sh new --slug globex --name "Globex Corporation" --domain platform.example.com --admin ciso@globex.com writes deploy/cells/globex.values.yaml from deploy/cells/_template.values.yaml . Edit it: image repositories and tag, TLS issuer, database (managed in production), backups (S3), SMTP, replicas. Commit it: deploy/cells/ is the inventory of cells. export DB_PASSWORD=… KC_ADMIN_PASSWORD=… # from the secret manager scripts/cell-provision.sh apply --slug globex --dry-run # preflight + render, nothing applied scripts/cell-provision.sh apply --slug globex # for real apply runs a preflight (every ${VAR} placeholder has a value, ingress class and ClusterIssuer exist, whether the three hostnames resolve yet), fills the placeholders into a temporary copy of the values file, runs helm upgrade --install , waits for the workloads with a progress line every 15 s (what is not ready yet, and a warning the moment something is stuck: ImagePullBackOff, CrashLoopBackOff, a pod Pending for minutes), on a new cell runs the first backup (an existing cell is backed up before the upgrade instead), then the checks : API and worker rolled out, no restarting pods, the API answers /api/v1/health/ready from inside the cluster, the backup CronJob exists; it prints the chart's notes and the handover pointers. make provision TENANT=globex is the same thing. apply deliberately does not use helm's own --wait . With backups on a PVC and a StorageClass whose volumeBindingMode is WaitForFirstConsumer (kind's standard , EKS gp3, GKE standard-rwo , AKS managed-csi ), the backups PVC stays Pending until the first backup Job mounts it, and helm install --wait waits for every PVC to be Bound: a plain helm install --wait or make deploy … --wait of this chart sits there until its timeout. The script waits for Deployments and StatefulSets instead, and the first backup it runs binds the PVC. First boot takes a few minutes: Keycloak imports the realm, the API's init container runs the migrations, the managed runner registers once the API answers (it retries with backoff). 4. Verify scripts/cell-provision.sh check --slug globex API=https://globex.platform.example.com/api/v1 KC=https://auth-globex.platform.example.com KC_USER=… KC_PASS=… scripts/smoke.sh make backup TENANT=globex # the first backup, downloaded and checksum-verified Then open https://globex.platform.example.com : the login goes to the cell's Keycloak. Until an IdP is configured there is no user to log in with on a production cell ( seedUsers: [] ), which is the next step. 5. Handover Identity. Open https://auth-globex.platform.example.com as the Keycloak admin ( KC_ADMIN_PASSWORD ), realm platform , and add the customer's identity provider (SAML or OIDC: Entra ID, Okta, Google…) with "first login flow" creating users. E-mail must be mapped: the platform keys users on it. First administrator. The person listed in tenant.adminEmails logs in; their first login grants ORG_ADMIN on the root organization (audit events organization.bootstrapped and membership.granted ). From there they invite the team (Members). Setup card. The Overview shows the organization setup to administrators: connect source code (GitHub App, GitLab…), check the managed runner, alerts, team. Service coverage shows what each service still lacks. Tell them what they own. Hostnames, the registry ( registry-globex.… , matelot registry login ), where backups go and how long they are kept, and the support channel. 6. Day 2 Upgrade one cell: change the tag in deploy/cells/<slug>.values.yaml and scripts/cell-provision.sh apply --slug <slug> (or apply --tag X for a one-off). apply takes a pre-upgrade backup first ( --no-backup to skip), then upgrades. Migrations run in the API's init container. An image release rolls only the api, worker, web and managed-runner pods: Postgres, Keycloak, Redis and the registry keep running (their pod templates carry no version label; make helm-lint asserts it). Upgrade all cells: for f in deploy/cells/*.values.yaml; do s=$(basename "$f" .values.yaml); [ "$s" = _template ] || scripts/cell-provision.sh apply --slug "$s" --tag X; done — one at a time, checks included, stops at the first unhealthy cell. Scale: api.replicas , web.replicas , managedRunners.replicas ; resources per component in the values file. Rotate the Keycloak admin password: change it in Keycloak, update the secret manager; the chart value is only the bootstrap value. Restore: docs/backup-restore.md. 7. Decommission scripts/cell-decommission.sh --slug globex # final backup to ./decommissioned/globex, helm uninstall; data kept scripts/cell-decommission.sh --slug globex --purge # … and delete the namespace with every volume Without --purge the namespace and its PVCs (Postgres, registry blobs, backups) and the kept Secrets stay for the retention period agreed with the customer; the script lists exactly what remains. --purge later (with the release already gone it skips the backup, deletes the namespace and waits for the PVs to disappear) removes them. Then remove deploy/cells/globex.values.yaml , the DNS records if any were specific, the S3 prefix after retention, and the customer-side IdP client. 8. Conventions Namespace tenant-<slug> , release <slug> , hosts <slug>.<domain> , auth-<slug>.<domain> , registry-<slug>.<domain> . One wildcard certificate per cell is not needed: cert-manager issues per host. Secrets generated by the chart (encryption key, registry token key pair, events secret, managed-runner secret) are created on the first install and reused on every upgrade; they are in every backup. Provide encryptionKey etc. explicitly only when migrating a cell from elsewhere. Resource defaults in the chart fit a small cell on one node; the template sets 20Gi volumes. Size up in the values file, never in the chart. Reference Piece Where Provision / check scripts/cell-provision.sh , make provision TENANT=… Decommission scripts/cell-decommission.sh , make decommission TENANT=… Cell inventory deploy/cells/<slug>.values.yaml (template _template.values.yaml ) Chart deploy/helm/secops-cell ( make helm-lint renders every supported configuration) Backups docs/backup-restore.md · Managed runners: docs/managed-runners.md · Usage: docs/usage-and-limits.md

title: Backup and restore
headings: Case 1: roll back the data of a running cell
Case 2: rebuild the cell on a new cluster (disaster recovery)
text: Backup and restore of a tenant cell A cell's state lives in three places: the platform database (everything the product shows), the Keycloak database (users, realm, sessions) and a handful of Kubernetes Secrets , one of which, the cell encryption key, is the only way to read the stored connection credentials (GitHub tokens, registry passwords, Jira tokens, SMTP…). A backup without the key restores a cell whose connections all say "cannot decrypt". The chart ships a scheduled backup that captures all three into one archive, and the repository ships the restore. What is in an archive <slug>-<UTC stamp>.tar.gz (plus .sha256 ): acme-20261009T021700Z/ manifest.txt cell, time, databases, pg_dump and server versions db/platform.dump pg_dump --format=custom (compressed, restorable with pg_restore) db/keycloak.dump secrets/acme-cell-key/CELL_ENCRYPTION_KEY secrets/acme-managed-runner/MANAGED_RUNNER_SECRET secrets/acme-registry/{registry.key,registry.crt,REGISTRY_EVENTS_SECRET,REGISTRY_HOST,…} secrets/acme-postgres/{POSTGRES_DB,POSTGRES_USER,POSTGRES_PASSWORD} secrets/acme-keycloak/{KC_BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_*,KC_DB_*} secrets/acme-api-secrets/{DATABASE_URL,REDIS_URL,GITHUB_APP_*} Not included: the registry's image blobs (PVC <release>-registry ). Images are rebuildable from source and the platform re-scans what is pushed; if you need them kept, back the registry's volume up with your storage's snapshots or run the registry on object storage. Redis holds only queues and caches. The archive is sensitive. It contains the encryption key, database passwords and the Keycloak admin password. Keep the PVC and the bucket restricted to the operators of the cell, turn on server-side encryption on the bucket, and never attach an archive to a ticket. Turning backups on backup: enabled: true schedule: "17 2 * * *" # cron, UTC retentionDays: 14 # archives older than this are pruned from the PVC pvc: { enabled: true, size: 10Gi } s3: # optional off-site copy of every archive enabled: true bucket: acme-cell-backups prefix: cells/acme region: eu-central-1 credentialsSecret: "" # Secret with AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID / AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, or empty for IRSA / workload identity endpoint: "" # S3-compatible endpoint for MinIO / Ceph make deploy (or helm upgrade ) creates the CronJob <release>-backup , the PVC <release>-backups (kept on uninstall) and the script ConfigMap. On a StorageClass with volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer (kind, EKS gp3, GKE, AKS defaults) that PVC stays Pending until the first backup runs — normal, but it means helm … --wait on this chart waits for it: use scripts/cell-provision.sh apply (which waits on the workloads and runs the first backup) or run make backup right after a plain install. The job runs pg_dump with the chart's own Postgres image, so client and server versions match. With S3, the dump is an init container and the upload the main container, so an upload never starts before the dump has finished. Retention on S3 is the bucket's lifecycle rule; the chart does not delete from buckets. For an external database ( postgres.bundled=false ) the job dumps the platform database through the API's DATABASE_URL . The Keycloak database of an external server is not dumped: rely on the managed database's own snapshots, which you should have anyway in that setup, or point a second CronJob at it. Verify the first run before trusting the schedule: make backup TENANT=acme # runs the job now, waits, downloads the archive to ./backups and checks its sha256 scripts/cell-backup.sh -r acme -n tenant-acme --list Both need kubectl access to the namespace. --download and --list use a short-lived pod that mounts the PVC, so they need backup.pvc.enabled . Restoring Everything goes through scripts/cell-restore.sh ( make restore TENANT=acme ARCHIVE=… ). It verifies the checksum, shows the manifest and asks for confirmation ( --yes to skip), then: recreates every Secret from the archive, with Helm's ownership labels so a later helm upgrade or helm install adopts them and, thanks to the chart's lookup-reuse, keeps their values; scales the API, worker, Keycloak and managed runners to 0 and waits for their pods to go; copies the dumps into the Postgres pod and, for each database, checks that the dump is readable, drops and recreates the database, and runs pg_restore ; a corrupt dump stops the restore before anything is dropped; scales everything back to the replica counts it found and waits for the API, whose init container applies any migrations newer than the backup. If anything fails the workloads are scaled back up (the EXIT trap), so a failed restore leaves the cell running on whatever the databases hold at that point: the old data when the failure was before the drop, so check the output. Case 1: roll back the data of a running cell make restore TENANT=acme ARCHIVE=backups/acme-20261009T021700Z.tar.gz Expect a few minutes of downtime: the cell is down from step 2 to step 4. Users' sessions survive only if the Keycloak dump is from the same realm, which it is for the cell's own backups. Case 2: rebuild the cell on a new cluster (disaster recovery) The order matters: the Secrets must exist before the first helm install , otherwise the chart generates a fresh encryption key and the restored connections cannot be decrypted. scripts/cell-restore.sh -r acme -n tenant-acme --secrets-only backups/acme-20261009T021700Z.tar.gz make deploy TENANT=acme # same values as before: slug, domain, images scripts/cell-restore.sh -r acme -n tenant-acme --databases-only backups/acme-20261009T021700Z.tar.gz --secrets-only creates the namespace's Secrets ( kubectl create namespace tenant-acme first if it does not exist). Then point DNS at the new ingress and re-register any self-hosted runners whose tokens were not in the backup (managed runners pick up the restored MANAGED_RUNNER_SECRET by themselves). Case 3: external database With postgres.bundled=false there is no Postgres pod. Stop the API, worker and Keycloak ( kubectl scale … --replicas=0 ), then from a machine that reaches the server: tar -xzf acme-20261009T021700Z.tar.gz PGHOST=globex-db.internal PGUSER=platform PGPASSWORD=… deploy/helm/secops-cell/files/restore-db.sh acme-20261009T021700Z/db and scale the workloads back. restore-db.sh takes the database names as extra arguments to restore only some of them. After any restore scripts/smoke.sh against the cell (login, create a workspace, read the audit trail). Connections page: every connection shows its status and none says "cannot decrypt". If they do, the restored CELL_ENCRYPTION_KEY is not the one the data was encrypted with: restore the Secrets from the right archive and restart the API. matelot runners list : managed runners online; self-hosted runners may need a new registration token. The audit trail records nothing about the restore itself (it happened below the API); note it in your change log. Testing the backup A backup that has never been restored is a hope, not a backup. Once a quarter, or before any risky upgrade: make backup TENANT=acme BACKUP_DIR=./drill helm install acme-drill deploy/helm/secops-cell -n tenant-acme-drill --create-namespace --set tenant.slug=acme-drill … scripts/cell-restore.sh -r acme-drill -n tenant-acme-drill ./drill/acme-….tar.gz The drill cell should show the same projects, connections and findings. Uninstall it afterwards and delete its namespace (the PVCs are kept on uninstall by design). Reference Piece Where Backup job script deploy/helm/secops-cell/files/backup.sh (ConfigMap <release>-backup-script ) In-database restore deploy/helm/secops-cell/files/restore-db.sh Operator scripts scripts/cell-backup.sh , scripts/cell-restore.sh ; make backup , make restore Chart values backup.* in values.yaml ; example in values-production.example.yaml

title: Usage and rate limits
text: Usage metering and rate limits Usage (Organization → Usage, matelot usage , GET /organizations/:id/usage ) Per organization and calendar month (UTC): Metric Definition Active seats Members of the organization (a role anywhere in its tree, account not disabled) who made at least one authenticated request that month — in the web app, with a personal token, or through MCP. CI tokens and runners are never seats; platform administrators without a role in the organization are not counted. Members Distinct people with a role in the organization's tree (not disabled), at computation time. Runner minutes Sum of finished − started for jobs run by a runner that finished in the month (also per job type). Platform jobs (policy evaluation) count as jobs but use no runner minutes. Jobs / Pipelines / SBOMs Finished jobs, pipelines started, SBOMs stored in the month. Projects / Services / Environments Inventory size (not archived) at computation time. The current month is computed live. The worker writes a snapshot of every organization's current month every hour and finalises the previous month on its first pass after the month ends, so history survives job and pipeline pruning. ?month=YYYY-MM selects a month, ?format=csv exports the 12-month history ( month,seats_active,seats_members,projects,services,environments,pipelines,jobs,runner_minutes,sboms ). Visible with audit:read (organization and security administrators, compliance officers, CISO, auditors). Rate limits Fixed one-minute windows per caller, counted in Redis (shared by all API replicas; if Redis is unreachable each process counts on its own and logs it once): Class Key Default / min Env read (GET/HEAD) user, or CI token 1200 RATE_LIMIT_READ_PER_MINUTE write user, or CI token 300 RATE_LIMIT_WRITE_PER_MINUTE runner runner 1200 RATE_LIMIT_RUNNER_PER_MINUTE anonymous client IP 120 RATE_LIMIT_ANONYMOUS_PER_MINUTE failed authentication (401) client IP 30 RATE_LIMIT_AUTH_FAILURES_PER_MINUTE 0 disables a class, RATE_LIMIT_ENABLED=false disables all. Successful requests to /health , /webhooks/* , /registry/token , /registry/events and /.well-known/* are never counted (docker pulls are bursty). Failed authentication is counted separately, on every path: a 401 (bad or expired bearer token, wrong docker-login password on /registry/token , bad webhook signature or registry events secret) counts against the client IP; past the limit the 401 becomes a 429 with Retry-After . Requests that authenticate are never affected by their address's failures. A 403 (authenticated, not allowed) counts against the caller's own read / write bucket. These are counted in the global exception filter, because the guards reject them before the rate-limit interceptor runs. Responses carry RateLimit-Limit , RateLimit-Remaining , RateLimit-Reset ; over the limit the API answers 429 with Retry-After . The request is refused before it runs, so the CLI (2.16.0+) waits for Retry-After (≤ 60 s, up to 3 times) and repeats it — also for writes.

title: Endpoints of a cell
text: Endpoints of a cell Every cell exposes exactly three public hostnames, all TLS, no ports: Surface Hostname Used by Web app + API ( /api/v1 ) https://<slug>.<domain> browsers, runners ( RUNNER_URL=https://<slug>.<domain>/api/v1 ), CI ( SECOPS_URL ), webhooks Container registry https://registry-<slug>.<domain> docker login/push/pull , runners scanning images, clusters pulling environment images Identity (Keycloak) https://auth-<slug>.<domain> browser login (OIDC), the API (JWKS) <slug> is the customer ( acme ), <domain> the operator's cell domain ( secops.example.com ). One wildcard certificate *.secops.example.com (or cert-manager per host) covers all three, because every name is a single level under the domain. The Helm chart derives all URLs from tenant.slug and tenant.domain : token realm, registry notifications, OIDC issuer, WEB_BASE_URL , GitHub App callback. Provisioning a cell therefore needs from the operator: three DNS records (or a wildcard), a TLS issuer, and helm install (M12 automates this in the cell provisioning flow). Nothing about ports or hostnames is configured by teams: the UI, the CI snippets and the CLI print the cell's real URLs. Local development make dev / make web / docker compose use http://localhost:3000 (API), :5173 (web), :8080 (Keycloak) and localhost:5000 (registry, insecure-registries in Docker Desktop). These never appear in a deployed cell.

title: ADR 1: tenancy and stack
headings: 1. One dedicated cell per client, operated by us
2. Keep organization scoping inside the cell
3. Keycloak per cell owns authentication; the platform owns authorization
5. Drizzle ORM with generated SQL migrations
6. Audit trail is a domain concern, not middleware
text: ADR 0001 — Tenancy model and core stack Status: accepted · Date: 2026-09-18 Context The product is a B2B security/compliance platform for enterprise clients who expect strong isolation, SSO/SAML integration and, frequently, their own compliance evidence about how their data is separated. We also need multiple organizations inside one client (parent company with subsidiaries, MSSP serving several customers) and an agentic AI layer whose actions must be attributable and permission-scoped. Decisions 1. One dedicated cell per client, operated by us Each client gets its own Kubernetes namespace ( tenant-<slug> ) holding the API, workers, Postgres, Redis and Keycloak, deployed as one Helm release of deploy/helm/secops-cell . A control plane (later) provisions cells and rolls versions across them. Why: physical isolation is easy to explain and audit; noisy-neighbour and blast-radius problems disappear; per-client versions and maintenance windows become possible; the Helm chart doubles as the on-prem/regulated-deployment story. Cost: fleet operations (upgrades, monitoring, cost per idle client). Accepted; it is the control plane's job. 2. Keep organization scoping inside the cell Organizations remain a first-class entity with a parent/child hierarchy, even though a cell serves one client. Parent-org roles apply inside child orgs. Why: subsidiaries and MSSP customers are per-client requirements, not cross-client ones. 3. Keycloak per cell owns authentication; the platform owns authorization Keycloak (realm platform ) issues RS256 tokens; the API validates them against the realm JWKS and provisions users just-in-time. Roles are not Keycloak roles: they are platform memberships ( user × role × scope ) because the permission model is hierarchical and resource-scoped. Why: SSO/SAML/OIDC brokering, MFA and session management are solved problems in Keycloak; authorization must understand the platform's hierarchy, which Keycloak does not. 4. TypeScript / NestJS Chosen by the team. Modules map 1:1 to the product's domains; DI makes the RBAC guard and audit service pervasive without boilerplate. 5. Drizzle ORM with generated SQL migrations Why over Prisma: no native query engine to ship (smaller images, faster cold start in cells), migrations are plain SQL under review, and the query builder stays close to SQL for the graph-style queries the security graph and risk engine will need. Migrations are applied by the API pod's init container, so an image rollout carries its schema. 6. Audit trail is a domain concern, not middleware Services write explicit audit events with before/after state and reason. The request id from x-request-id is stored with each event so logs and audit rows correlate. Consequences Every new domain follows the same template: schema in schema.ts , permissions declared in permissions.ts , controller routes with @RequirePermission , service methods that audit. The agent layer (step 7) will act through the same API with a service identity whose memberships bound what it may touch; actor_type = AI_AGENT is already in the schema.

title: ADR 2: web app
text: ADR 0002 — Web app: React on the TailAdmin template, runtime configuration Status: accepted · Date: 2026-09-18 Context The team chose React for the frontend and, after trying an MUI-based kit, the TailAdmin React template (MIT; React 19, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS v4) as the base: all TypeScript, dark mode and a collapsible sidebar built in, and small readable primitives instead of a component framework. Decisions TailAdmin kept as the presentation layer; product code separated. src/layout , src/components , src/context and src/icons are the template, adapted where the product needs it (sidebar menu, header controls, user menu, brand). src/platform and src/pages are ours. Styling is Tailwind utility classes using the template's design tokens ( src/index.css ). Same origin as the API. In a cell the ingress routes /api to the API and / to the web app; in development Vite proxies /api . No CORS configuration is needed for the first-party UI and cookies/tokens never cross origins. Runtime configuration via /config.json . One image serves every cell; the ConfigMap holds the Keycloak URL, realm, client id and product name. Authentication in the browser with oidc-client-ts (authorization code + PKCE against the platform-web public client). Tokens live in session storage; the API remains the only place authorization is decided. Data access through TanStack Query with a global refresh interval (the "Update every" control), so every section polls the same way LiveDashboard does. Consequences New sections = a page component + hooks; no build-time environment variables. Visual changes use the template's Tailwind tokens ( src/index.css ); no separate stylesheet. test/render.mjs mounts the whole app in jsdom in CI; keep it green when adding pages. Later, Vulnerabilities/SBOM/Policies/Compliance replace their muted tabs with pages.

title: ADR 3: two-level RBAC
text: ADR 0003 — Two-level access control (GitLab model) Status: accepted · Date: 2026-09-18 Decision Access control has two levels, like GitLab's instance admins + group/project access levels. Cell level (instance). Every user is user or admin ( users.platform_role ). Administrators see and can do everything in the cell and own the Administration area (users, and from step 02/03 on: integrations, runners, cell settings). Users see nothing until they hold a role somewhere. Admins can disable a user (they keep their memberships but cannot sign in). Bootstrap emails ( BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_EMAILS ) become administrators on first sign-in and owners ( ORG_ADMIN ) of the root organization. Scoped level. Memberships = user × role × scope at organization, workspace, team, project, service or environment. A role applies to its scope and everything below (groups → subgroups → projects); the effective permissions at a point are the union of all roles up the chain (GitLab's "highest access level wins"); nothing flows upward; a member can always see the path to what they own. Roles are the concept's eleven ( ORG_ADMIN = owner of a subtree, TEAM_LEAD ≈ maintainer, DEVELOPER , READ_ONLY ≈ reporter, plus the security/compliance roles). Why Enterprise expectation and a model every developer already understands. The cell admin is the operator's and customer IT's handle on the instance without granting organization roles that show up in security dashboards. Scoped roles keep least privilege for everyone else, including the AI (step 15 inherits them). Consequences AccessContext.isPlatformAdmin short-circuits AuthorizationService ; every listing that filters by visibility automatically includes everything for admins. Guards must not assume an admin holds any membership; audit shows admin actions as the user. Cell-level actions ( user.* ) are audited without an organization id.
